For the treatment of Bartonella-associated endocarditis, the preferred regimen includes gentamicin at a dose of 3 mg/kg/day administered intravenously every 8 hours for 14 days, combined with ceftriaxone at 2 g intravenously every 24 hours for 6 weeks. Doxycycline at 100 mg orally twice daily for 6 weeks may be added as an optional component. 2. For Verruga peruana, the preferred treatment is azithromycin at 500 mg orally once daily for 7 days. Alternative regimens include rifampin at 600 mg orally once daily for 14–21 days or ciprofloxacin at 500 mg orally twice daily for 7–10 days. 3. For bacillary peliosis, the first preferred regimen is erythromycin at 500 mg orally four times daily for a minimum of 4 months. The second preferred regimen is doxycycline at 100 mg orally twice daily for at least 4 months. 4. In cases of neurocysticercosis with cysticercal encephalitis (characterized by diffuse cerebral edema and multiple inflamed cysticerci), antiparasitic therapy is contraindicated. This is because enhanced parasite killing can worsen the host's inflammatory response, potentially leading to diffuse cerebral edema and transtentorial herniation. 5. Radiographic evidence of calcified cysts in neurocysticercosis is a significant risk factor for recurrent seizure activity. These lesions are present in approximately 10% of individuals in endemic regions. Seizures in these patients should be managed with antiepileptic therapy. 6. For subarachnoid cysts in neurocysticercosis, the preferred treatment includes albendazole at 15 mg/kg/day orally in two divided doses for 28 days, combined with prednisone (up to 60 mg/day orally) or dexamethasone (up to 24 mg/day). The corticosteroid dose can often be tapered after a few weeks. 7. Giant cysticerci, which are typically associated with cerebral edema and mass effect, should be managed with high-dose corticosteroids, with or without mannitol. 8. For ocular cysticercosis, surgical excision is indicated for intraocular cysts. Cysticercal involvement of the extraocular muscles should be treated with albendazole and corticosteroids. 9. Spinal cysticercosis should be managed with medical therapy, including corticosteroids and antiparasitic drugs. 10. Body lice infestations are treated by improving personal hygiene, including ensuring regular (at least weekly) changes of clean clothes. Clothing, bedding, and towels used by the infested person should be laundered in hot water (at least 130°F) and machine-dried on the hot cycle. In some cases, a pediculicide such as ivermectin lotion may be used, but this is generally unnecessary if hygiene is maintained and items are laundered appropriately. If ivermectin lotion is used, it should be applied as directed on the bottle or by a physician. A 5% lotion (e.g., Ovide) should be applied to dry hair for 8–12 hours, followed by shampooing, with two doses given 7–9 days apart. Alternatively, oral ivermectin at 200 μg/kg as a single dose, repeated at 7-day intervals for three doses, has been reported as effective. 11. Myiasis, caused by fly larvae, requires surgical removal of the larvae. Preferred treatments include occluding the punctum to prevent gas exchange using substances like petrolatum, fingernail polish, makeup cream, or bacon. When the larvae migrate, they should be manually removed. Myiasis typically presents as a cutaneous or subcutaneous nodule with a central punctum. 12. For scabies in adults, the preferred treatment is permethrin 5% cream applied to all areas of the body from the neck down and washed off after 8–14 hours. Alternatively, oral ivermectin at 200 μg/kg can be given once and repeated in 2 weeks. Another option is lindane (1%) lotion or cream applied in a thin layer to all areas of the body from the neck down and washed off after 8 hours. 13. For infants and young children with scabies, the preferred treatment is permethrin 5% cream applied to all areas of the body from the neck down and washed off after 8–14 hours. Lindane should not be used in children under 10 years of age. 14. Norwegian scabies, an aggressive infestation often seen in immunodeficient, debilitated, or malnourished individuals, requires a combination of topical scabicides (such as 5% benzyl benzoate or 5% permethrin cream applied to the entire body daily for 7 days, then twice weekly until cure) and oral ivermectin at 200 μg/kg on days 1, 2, 8, 9, and 15. 15. For pregnant or lactating women with scabies, the preferred treatment is permethrin 5% cream applied to all areas of the body from the neck down and washed off after 8–14 hours.
